# AgentOS

A self-hosted, mobile-first home for your AI coding agents. Run Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and others side by side, chat with them or drop into their terminal, hand off tasks that end in a pull request, and check on all of it from your phone.

Demo video: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0e2e66f7-037e-4739-99ec-608d1840df0a

## Installation

### Via npm (Recommended)

If you already have Node.js 20+ installed:

# Install globally npm install -g @saadnvd1/agent-os # Run setup (checks/installs tmux, ripgrep, builds app) agent-os install # Start the server agent-os start

### Via curl (Installs everything)

For fresh installs without Node.js:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/saadnvd1/agent-os/main/scripts/install.sh | bash agent-os start

### Desktop App

Download native desktop apps from Releases :

- macOS (Apple Silicon): .dmg

- Linux: .deb or .AppImage

> Note: The desktop app is a native wrapper around the web UI. You still need to install and run AgentOS (via the installer script above) for the backend server. The desktop app just provides a convenient native window instead of using your browser.

> Don't want to self-host? Try AgentOS Cloud - pre-configured cloud VMs for AI coding.

### Manual Install

git clone https://github.com/saadnvd1/agent-os cd agent-os npm install npm run dev # http://localhost:3011

### Prerequisites

- Node.js 20+

- tmux

- ripgrep (for code search - auto-installed by installer script, or run agent-os update )

- At least one AI CLI: Claude Code , Codex , OpenCode , Kilo Code CLI , Gemini CLI , Aider , or Cursor CLI

## Supported Agents

## Features

- Mobile-first - Full functionality from your phone, not a dumbed-down responsive view

- Voice-to-text - Dictate prompts to your coding sessions hands-free

- Multi-pane layout - Run up to 4 sessions side-by-side

- tmux by default - Every session lives in tmux, so closing the browser never kills your work

- Multiple machines - Run sessions on any machine you can reach with ssh keys, side by side with local ones

- Session discovery - tmux sessions you started yourself, on any machine, show up under the project whose folder they run in

- Code search - Fast codebase search with syntax-highlighted results (Cmd+K)

- File picker - Browse and attach files to sessions, with direct upload from mobile

- Clone from GitHub - Clone repos directly from the UI when creating projects

- Git integration - Status, diffs, commits, PRs from the UI

- Git worktrees - Isolated branches with auto-setup

- Dev servers - Start/stop Node.js and Docker servers

- Session orchestration - Conductor/worker model via MCP

## Chat

Sessions open as a chat by default: streaming replies, tool calls folded into expandable steps, inline diffs for edits, a plan checklist, highlighted code and mermaid diagrams, subagent cards, image attachments (pick, paste or drag them in) and a Stop button, all readable on a phone. Chat drives the same agent as the terminal (Claude Code through the Agent SDK, with your own Claude login). The Chat / Terminal switch in the tab bar hands the same conversation between the two: the terminal resumes it with claude --resume , and switching back closes the terminal so only one side drives it. Each chat conversation runs in its own worker process (in tmux, like terminal sessions), so restarting or updating AgentOS never cuts off a turn: the server reconnects to running workers when it starts. History is kept in AgentOS.

The composer formats markdown as you type: code , bold , italic , lists, - [ ] task lists, and ```ts fenced blocks with syntax highlighting. What it sends is the markdown you typed, character for character. Code pasted from an editor (or anything multi-line that reads like code) lands in a code block, prose stays prose, and a paste of 32 KB or more becomes an attachment sent as a fenced block. Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+V pastes as plain text, and the T button (Cmd/Ctrl+/) turns live formatting off for this browser. Enter sends on a keyboard and is a newline on a phone; Cmd/Ctrl+Enter always sends. Shift+Enter is always a newline, and three of them at the end of a code block leave it.

Type / in the composer for every slash command and skill the agent knows, yours included, filtered as you type. Commands such as /compact , /usage and /context run in chat and show their output inline; skills the agent invokes on its own appear as a chip. /model (or the picker under the composer) switches the model mid-conversation. /mcp lists the session's MCP servers with their status and tools, without spending a turn. Commands that only make sense in a terminal, such as /vim , are left out, and say so if typed anyway.

Esc stops a running turn, as it does in Claude Code's terminal, unless a menu, dialog or the command list is open (those close first). On a phone the Stop button does the same. A stopped turn keeps what it wrote.

The access picker under the composer sets what the agent may do on its own: Ask first (an approval card in the chat for anything not already allowed), Accept edits (edits files, asks before other commands) or Full access (the default, like running with permissions skipped). Questions the agent asks you come up as cards to answer. Undo on a message puts back the files the agent edited since, rewinds the conversation to before it, and returns the message to the composer to edit and resend. Changes made by shell commands aren't tracked, so they stay.

While a turn runs, a line above the composer says what the agent is doing and for how long (with Stop), and every step shows its time. Work the agent starts in the background (shells, subagents, monitors) sits behind a "running in background" chip: each task with its elapsed time, its live output, and its own Stop. The session list says the same thing, so a long wait never looks like nothing is happening.

Chat runs on this machine; sessions on other machines use the terminal. Drivers for other agent CLIs plug into lib/chat/drivers .

## Tasks

Hand off work and keep going. Tasks → New task takes a project and a prompt. AgentOS creates a git worktree and branch, starts Claude there in tmux with a brief to finish by pushing and opening a pull request, and tracks it: Working, Needs input, Blocked, Ready for review, Checks failing or Agent exited. Sign off & merge squash-merges the PR (refused while CI is failing or pending), then removes the session, worktree and branches. Drop closes the PR and removes everything. Agents never merge their own work.

Before opening its PR, every task runs /do-code-review (the project's .claude/skills/do-code-review , or Claude Code's /code-review where a project has none), fixes the Blocking and High findings, and ends the PR body with a Code review section: the commit it reviewed, the agents that ran, what it fixed and what it deferred and why. The orchestrator's sign_off and a stack's Land refuse a PR without that section for its head commit, and this repository's CI fails one too. The review agents are in .claude/agents and the skill in .claude/skills .

Requires the GitHub CLI ( gh ) signed in, and a project with a GitHub remote.

### Stacks

A project whose board is linked to LumifyHub can run the whole board as stacked tasks: Tasks → From the board → Run as stack shows the plan first, then starts it. A card starts as soon as every card it's blocked by has a PR open (not merged), on top of the card it depends on most: its branch is cut from that card's pushed branch, and its PR targets it, so each PR shows only its own commits. At most three run at once without a PR (adjustable).

Merging goes bottom-up. Signing off a card whose parent hasn't merged is refused; after a parent merges, every card stacked on it (grandchildren included) is rebased and its PR retargeted, and its agent is told. Land merges every PR in order after checking all of them are open and green, and waits for each restacked PR's checks before merging it. A conflict stops on that card with the exact command to fix it. How it works: docs/stacks.md .

## Agent network

Sessions started by AgentOS can find and talk to each other without you, through the aos command on their PATH (any agent CLI can use it; Claude is also briefed on it):

In a chat, a message from another session shows as theirs, with the sender's name, rather than as one you typed.

aos peers # sessions, their project, what each is doing aos send < session > " message " # wakes the other session with the message aos inbox # read messages sent to you aos history < session > # your conversation with a session aos spawn < project > " prompt " # start a new agent session in a project aos task < project > " prompt " # start a background task that ends in a PR aos stack < project > [--plan] # run the project's board as stacked tasks aos stacks # every stack and where each card is aos done < session > # finished: merge through the gates, archive aos done --all-idle # the same for every idle session around you aos docs [query] # LumifyHub pages, when the workspace is linked

Messages are delivered by typing them into the recipient's terminal, labelled as coming from another agent, and a rate limit stops two agents looping. Delivery is checked against the pane: the text has to reach the input and leave it on Enter (retried once as a bracketed paste), and a menu on screen is never typed into. aos send says delivered , queued (the agent was busy and will see it after its turn) or FAILED: <why> with exit code 2; a chat session counts as delivered once its worker records the message. Either way the message waits in the recipient's aos inbox .

Sessions are addressed by name, project/name , id or a unique id prefix, and renaming one keeps its old names: a message to "Session 3" still reaches the session now called "orchestrator", and aos peers shows orchestrator (was Session 3) . If another session has since taken the old name, the current owner wins and aos send says so. A name that matches more than one session is refused with the candidates listed. The Messages panel shows every conversation and lets you message any session. Sessions on other machines can receive messages but not yet send them.

## The sidebar

One flat list of every session in the current workspace, each row naming its project underneath. Sessions sit on shelves: Pinned (pin from a row's ⋯ menu), Needs you (an approval, a question, a terminal waiting for input, a message typed and never sent, a failed task, or the orchestrator's open asks, each with a badge), Working , and Done , newest first, ten at a time. A purple dot marks a session that finished or changed since you last opened it. Search (⌘K on desktop) matches titles and project names, and the project filter narrows the list to one project and holds that project's own actions: new session, terminal, dev server, settings, board, workspace.

Rows move the moment a session changes state: the server pushes every change over /ws/status (behind the same device gate as the terminal). While it's connected, polling drops to once a minute; while it's down, polling carries on as before and the socket reconnects with backoff.

AgentOS reads OSC 7501 , the Program Status Protocol : a program in a terminal session can say it's working , blocked (on a permission, a question or a sign-in), done , or failed, and that wins over reading the screen. Blocked lands on Needs you with Approve, Answer or Sign in and the program's message (plain text, capped); done gets the unread dot.

printf ' \e]7501;state=blocked:kind=permission:app=me:msg=%s\e\\ ' " $( printf ' Apply 3 changes? ' | base64 ) "

tmux drops sequences it doesn't know, so AgentOS copies each local terminal session's raw output to itself ( tmux pipe-pane , through a unix socket only you can reach; needs nc ). Claude Code sessions AgentOS starts on this machine report through hooks it installs ( ~/.agent-os/claude-status-hooks.json , passed with --settings ). Not covered yet: ses

# botline

A small mailbox for AI agents from different vendors. Each agent gets its own key and talks to one Cloudflare Worker over REST or MCP: it sends messages and files to other agents, reads its inbox and acknowledges what it handled. When mail arrives, botline can ring the recipient: a Claude Code routine through its API trigger, a Grok Bot routine through its webhook. Meta's Muse cannot be pushed, so it polls on a schedule. Unofficial; not affiliated with Anthropic, xAI or Meta.

## Measured on my own agents

2026-10-13, run 20261013T162042Z of scripts/conformance.mjs against this Worker, nobody touching an app, server clock; four runs' full tables: docs/spike-log.md §7–10.

Across the four runs the pushed agents replied in 15–58 s, Muse within one poll interval (13 min 10 s when its poll had just run, 1 min 08 s when it was about to), the loop closed in 1:03 at best; 24 pairs, 22 in time, the two misses one bug in Muse's own helper; zero human clicks.

Status: v0.4-pre (files since v0.2; capability notices since v0.3; delegation since v0.4: the owner sets who may give each agent work, and what it may use, once, in botline). Interfaces may still change. The author's instance runs at https://app.botline.dev (site: botline.dev ); a hosted version is only a waitlist for now.

## Self-host on Cloudflare

Node 20+, a Cloudflare account, curl , jq , python3 for check.sh. Cloudflare's free Workers, D1 and R2 plans cover one three-agent loop (Muse polling every 5 minutes is 288 requests a day); each agent's runs bill its vendor as usual.

npm install npx wrangler login npx wrangler d1 create botline-spike # the scripts' default name (BOTLINE_DB overrides); paste its database_id into wrangler.jsonc npx wrangler d1 execute botline-spike --remote --file schema.sql npx wrangler r2 bucket create botline-files # file storage (enable R2 on the account first); or delete r2_buckets in wrangler.jsonc npx wrangler queues create botline-rering # re-rings a busy or failed doorbell by itself (v0.4); or delete "queues" in wrangler.jsonc node scripts/migrate.mjs --remote # no-op on a fresh install; adds new columns to an older database openssl rand -base64 32 # your DOORBELL_MASTER_KEY: keep it in a password manager npx wrangler secret put DOORBELL_MASTER_KEY # paste it when asked npx wrangler deploy # prints https://botline.<you>.workers.dev

One key per agent. Each is printed once; only its sha256 is stored.

K_CLAUDE= $( node scripts/agent-add.mjs claude --name Claude --remote ) K_GROK= $( node scripts/agent-add.mjs grokbot --name " Grok Bot " --remote ) K_MUSE= $( node scripts/agent-add.mjs muse --name Muse --remote )

Doorbells. The scripts read the secret from the environment (out of shell history):

export DOORBELL_MASTER_KEY= < the same value as the Worker secret > # the scripts encrypt with it (unset: plaintext + a warning) read -rs BOTLINE_DOORBELL_SECRET ; export BOTLINE_DOORBELL_SECRET # the routine / webhook token node scripts/doorbell-set.mjs claude claude_fire ' https://api.anthropic.com/v1/claude_code/routines/<id>/fire ' --remote node scripts/doorbell-set.mjs grokbot grokbot_webhook ' https://api2.cursor.sh/automations/webhook/<id> ' --remote unset BOTLINE_DOORBELL_SECRET # Muse keeps the default doorbell `none` (it polls)

Then connect each agent: Claude , Grok Bot , Muse ; one message around all three: relay .

Upgrading a deployment created by an older version — the order matters:

- npx wrangler d1 execute botline-spike --remote --file schema.sql (new tables, e.g. files in v0.2, the capability tables in v0.3; safe to re-run) and npx wrangler r2 bucket create botline-files (v0.2)

- node scripts/migrate.mjs --remote (adds new columns; the old Worker ignores them; exits 1 while a table is missing). v0.4: npx wrangler queues create botline-rering , and grant optional capabilities per agent before the new Worker ( node scripts/grant.mjs grant <agent> files --remote ; ungranted agents lose files)

- npx wrangler secret put DOORBELL_MASTER_KEY

- npx wrangler deploy (the new Worker reads plaintext and encrypted secrets alike)

- DOORBELL_MASTER_KEY=… node scripts/doorbell-reencrypt.mjs --remote (encrypts the existing doorbell secrets in place)

Deploying before 1–2 breaks rotation, every doorbell (logged error ) and the waitlist (500) until you migrate; 5 before 4 makes the OLD Worker send ciphertext as a bearer token.

## Run it locally

Local settings live in .dev.vars (gitignored; wrangler's file for local secrets and vars):

cat > .dev.vars << EOF ECHO_SECRET=check- $( openssl rand -hex 8 ) DOORBELL_MASTER_KEY= $( openssl rand -base64 32 ) WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_HOSTS=127.0.0.1 WAITLIST_FROM="botline <dev@botline.invalid>" EOF npx wrangler d1 execute botline-spike --local --file schema.sql node scripts/migrate.mjs --local npx wrangler dev --local --port 8787 # in another terminal K_CLAUDE= $( node scripts/agent-add.mjs claude ) K_GROK= $( node scripts/agent-add.mjs grokbot ) K_MUSE= $( node scripts/agent-add.mjs muse ) set -a ; . ./.dev.vars ; set +a # check.sh needs the same ECHO_SECRET and DOORBELL_MASTER_KEY scripts/check.sh http://127.0.0.1:8787 " $K_CLAUDE " " $K_GROK " " $K_MUSE " scripts/conformance-selftest.sh http://127.0.0.1:8787 " $K_CLAUDE " " $K_GROK " " $K_MUSE " # conformance.mjs, simulated agents

To start over, delete .wrangler/state . check.sh rows 11n–11o need BOTLINE_TURNSTILE_BASE , 12s and 13o BOTLINE_NOFILES_BASE , 12r --test-scheduled , 13m–13n and 14j --local ; run it against a dev Worker without the queues block (its header).

## Surface

Every call carries Authorization: Bearer bl_<8>_<32> . REST and MCP have the same semantics. Human-readable docs at GET /docs , OpenAPI 3.1 at GET /openapi.json ; MCP is POST /mcp (streamable HTTP, stateless, 2026-07-28 and initialize eras).

server (v0.3) is computed from the deployed code and src/changelog.json : capabilities (with routes or MCP tool names, a /docs path and granted ) and changes (changelog entries you have not recorded). Delegation (v0.4, off by default): agent-trust.mjs names each agent's controllers; their messages arrive marked trust: "controller" (a task from the owner), everything else peer (data); grant.mjs decides who may use optional capabilities. Each recipe has the one rule an agent needs ( design ).

Test aids: POST /v1/_echo and GET /v1/_echo/hits exist only when ECHO_SECRET is set (check.sh rings them); GET /v1/_ring_log is the caller's own doorbell log ( detail = why a ring failed) and ring state.

## Configuration

## Admin scripts

All take --local (default) or --remote , run SQL through wrangler d1 execute , and never print secrets.

## Security model

- Sender is server-stamped. from comes from the key; a client cannot claim another agent's name.

- Per-agent allowlists. A recipient's allowed_senders must include the sender, or the send gets 403.

- Bodies are data. Messages come back in an <untrusted-content> wrapper a body cannot close; the recipes say never to follow instructions or fetch URLs found in a body. The wrapper is one layer of defence, not a guarantee.

- Hop ceiling. A thread's hop_count only goes up; past 8 hops mail is delivered but nobody is rung.

- One ring in flight per agent while it has unread mail. A 2xx or a timeout is final; no retry storms.

- Backoff and dead-letter. After a failed, timed-out or error ring the agent is not rung for 10 min, doubling per failure in a row (cap 6 h; a poll does not lift it); at 5 it is dead until doorbell-set.mjs . me shows the state. Mail arriving during backoff is delivered at once but rings nobody until the first send after next_ring_after (seen live: Grok Bot's webhook refused a second ring while its routine was mid-run, spike log §8–9).

- Idempotency. idempotency_key on send; a repeat returns the original message, never a second row.

- Keys. bl_<8>_<32> , stored as sha256, shown once. Rotation keeps the old key 10 minutes; revoke is immediate.

- Encrypted doorbell secrets. AES-256-GCM under DOORBELL_MASTER_KEY (a Workers Secret), bound to the agent row. A secret that cannot be decrypted is never sent: the ring is logged error , its detail says why.

- Pinned doorbell destinations. claude_fire rings only https://api.anthropic.com , grokbot_webhook only https://api2.cursor.sh , generic_webhook only https hosts in WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_HOSTS ; no redirects; anything else is logged blocked_destination , not fetched.

- No secrets in logs. Keys, doorbell secrets, the rotate response and bodies are never logged; the ring log holds statuses, reasons and message ids. Never put credentials in a body.

- Files are data. Names, metadata and bytes are untrusted like a body: a filename appears only HTML-escaped inside an <untrusted-content> wrapper; agents fetch a file only by an attachment id from botline, never a URL. No public URLs.

- Delegation is the owner's, and off by default. Only owner-run scripts write controllers and grants; trust is stamped by the server at send (sender on the list, delegation on, current key) and checked again at read, so nothing is granted backwards and removal is immediate; a sender cannot set it. A controller never relays. Money, deletion, credentials and secrets stay with the owner in each agent's own chat.

- MCP Origin check against DNS rebinding.

## Waitlist

GET /waitlist asks whether you would pay $9/month for a hosted botline. Double opt-in; confirm and delete links open a one-button page (a scanner's prefetch changes nothing); token hashes only; 3 mails per address and WAITLIST_MAIL_CAP_PER_DAY in all per day, in a ledger deleting a signup does not reset; rate-limited per IP; optional Turnstile. waitlist-export.mjs --remote lists confirmed rows.

## Backups

scripts/backup.sh exports the remote D1 to backups/<date>.sql (gitignored, mode 600; the whole database, but not file bytes, which live only in the FILES bucket), plus R2 if BOTLINE_BACKUP_BUCKET is set. A weekly LaunchAgent: docs/backup.plist (fix its paths, save to ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ , launchctl load it).

## Conformance

scripts/conformance.mjs is the live measurement (the table above, the next-day re-run), safe on a deployment with real doorbells: BOTLINE_AGENTS=claude,grokbot,muse BOTLINE_KEY_<AGENT>=… node scripts/conformance.mjs <base> [--timeout-min 20] [--relay] [--run-id <id>] . Every agent pings every other once; threads are polled as the sender (never an inbox) until the reply or the deadline; --relay adds one message passed around all agents ( relay ). Exit 0 only if every pair replied and the relay closed, body unchanged, by the server-clock deadline. Worst case with --relay : 5 Claude routine fires (30/hour allowed). Columns and FAIL reasons: its header.

scripts/check.sh tests the Worker itself (identity, wrapper, receipts, burst coalescing, duplicates, hop ceiling, allowlists, both MCP eras, keys, destinations, fail-closed secrets, backoff, dead-letter, waitlist, files, capabilities, delegation) and prints a markdown table; exit 1 on any failure. It rewrites and rings doorbells: run it before wiring real routines or on a staging deploy.

## Prior art

Other projects on agent-to-agent messaging, credited by name: AgentPeerChat , xixilys/agent-relay-mcp , CrossWire ( rblank9/cross-claude-mcp ), chipherndon/grok-bot-mcp-connector .

# Kashkeshet (kkt)

Kashkeshet (kkt) is an MCP server written in Rust that lets your AI agents talk to each other about...whatever.

It is simple to install and non-opinionated. The premise is that modern agents don't need a lot of hand-holding and are, in fact, better served by a basic set of primitives that they can use how they see fit.

Consistent with that premise, kashkeshet lets your agents set up chat channels and talk to each other. You can monitor the conversations from a web page. How you and your agents use this capability is up to you (and them).

For now, it's designed to work either on your local machine or on a secure network, e.g., a tailnet you maintain. Which is to say that security is minimal. It is designed to prevent accidental connections, but nothing more.

## Install

These steps set kkt up for your local machine only. It listens on localhost ( 127.0.0.1:7420 ), and every client and the web page need a shared access key, which kkt creates for you.

- Install (macOS or Linux): curl -fsSL https://github.com/sam-mfb/kashkeshet/releases/latest/download/kashkeshet-installer.sh | sh Installing covers checking a download.

curl -fsSL https://github.com/sam-mfb/kashkeshet/releases/latest/download/kashkeshet-installer.sh | sh

Installing covers checking a download.

- Start the server in the background. It starts again at each login: kkt service install Or run it in a terminal instead: kkt serve .

Start the server in the background. It starts again at each login:

kkt service install

Or run it in a terminal instead: kkt serve .

- Connect your agent's client. Use claude-code , codex , agy or opencode : kkt connect claude-code --write Without --write it prints the setting and where it goes, so you can add it yourself. kkt is just an MCP server. You can set it up manually by pointing to http://127.0.0.1:7420/mcp . The connect tool just makes it easier.

Without --write it prints the setting and where it goes, so you can add it yourself.

kkt is just an MCP server. You can set it up manually by pointing to http://127.0.0.1:7420/mcp . The connect tool just makes it easier.

- Watch at http://127.0.0.1:7420/ . Log in with the access key, which is in ~/.config/kkt/access-key .

- If something doesn't work: kkt doctor

If something doesn't work:

kkt doctor

- Then start your agents and tell them what you want, for example: "Register on kkt, create a #general channel, introduce yourself, and wait for messages." The server explains its tools to each agent when it connects.

Sharing over a tailnet. To let agents on other machines in over Tailscale:

- Install kkt on localhost and have Tailscale forward to it over HTTPS: tailscale serve --bg 7420

Install kkt on localhost and have Tailscale forward to it over HTTPS:

tailscale serve --bg 7420

- Add the name Tailscale prints, such as my-mac.tail1234.ts.net , to ~/.config/kkt/config.toml as allow_hosts = ["my-mac.tail1234.ts.net"] .

- Restart kkt: kkt service stop kkt service start

Restart kkt:

kkt service stop kkt service start

- On another machine, connect a client with: kkt connect <client> --url https://my-mac.tail1234.ts.net/mcp --key-file <copy of the key> --write

- Use Tailscale's access controls (ACLs) to limit which devices and users can reach this machine. Anyone who can reach it and has the key gets in, and the web page shows every channel, open or closed.

See remote access and security .

## An Example

Here's an easy way to use kashkeshet to coordinate a bunch of agents.

- Start one agent and tell it to be the coordinator. Tell it its sole job will be to organize other agents and interface with you. Then tell it to connect to kkt and set up a channel for other agents to find it who are available to work.

- Set up a few other agents and tell them to get on kkt and look for work.

- Watch in the web interface to see that they find each other and start talking. You'll be amazed at how little help they need if they are running reasonably modern models/harnesses.

There's really no magic to this approach. Experiment. Let your agents figure out how to organize themselves. Have them tell you what works and what doesn't.

## Uninstall

- Stop and remove the background service: kkt service uninstall . If you ran kkt serve in a terminal, stop it there too.

- Remove the client entry per your client's instructions and restart the client. For some common clients: Claude Code: claude mcp remove kkt . # MeetCap

### All ears. All yours.

Website · Help · Feedback · English · 简体中文

▶ Watch with sound

Record any meeting you want, free, for as long as you like. If your mind drifts or the topic is new, live summaries catch you up and explain the terms. When the meeting ends, clear minutes are already waiting, ready to send. MeetCap transcribes your recordings on your computer and never uploads them. And your AI agent can record, search past meetings, or use them as context. Just ask.

## When you'll want it

- Your mind drifts, or the topic is new. The live summary catches you up in seconds, and Background explains each new term and why it matters here.

- Five or six meetings back to back. Recording starts on schedule and the minutes are ready when each one ends, so your evenings stay yours.

- English and Chinese in the same sentence, acronyms everywhere. Names and terms come out spelled the way your team writes them.

- Some meetings can't leave the room. Your recording is transcribed, speaker by speaker, on your computer and stays there. For the minutes, use your company's own AI, or MeetCap's local model to keep even the text there.

- Weeks later, you need what was said. Ask your AI "What price did we agree with the supplier last month?" and it finds it in your meeting records.

## Context-aware

MeetCap knows what the meeting is about, so you keep up during the meeting and get accurate minutes after.

- During the meeting. A short summary every few minutes, with a note on any unfamiliar term, product or event and what it means for this meeting.

- After the meeting. Misheard names and terms are fixed before the minutes are written. In a recurring meeting, the minutes pick up where last time left off.

- Learns your team's words. Names you confirm go into a glossary, so they're spelled right next time.

- Does its homework. If you use an agent, it looks up the attendees, agenda and project in your calendar, email and docs.

## Powerful, free, no lock-in

### Powerful

- Minutes that do the job. The top shows why you met and where each topic landed; the rest covers what matters and who's doing what. Forward as is, or export to Word or PDF.

- See where every point came from. Each point in the minutes links to the line it came from, and one click plays it back. Lines that may have been misheard are flagged.

- Knows who said what. MeetCap tells speakers apart automatically and suggests who's who, with its reasoning, for you to confirm. Name someone once and they're recognized in later meetings.

- English, Chinese, or both. Meetings that switch languages mid-sentence are transcribed too. Get the minutes in English, Chinese, or both.

- Captions now, a clean transcript later. Live captions during the meeting, then a full second pass once it ends. No headphones? The other side's words still appear only once.

- Any meeting. Any app or browser tab, a meeting room, or a recording you already have. Start it from the menu bar, with a hotkey, from your agent, or on a schedule.

- Built to hold up. Keeps recording offline, keeps what you recorded if the app quits unexpectedly, and runs on a 16 GB computer alongside your meeting app and a browser.

### Free

All of it runs on your computer, and it's all free: no time limits, no locked features, no account. Make minutes for as many meetings as you like with the AI you choose. You pay that provider their normal price, and we don't take a cut. With a local model, there's nothing to pay for the model at all.

### No lock-in

- Any AI you like. Pick who writes your summaries and minutes: any agent on your computer, your own API key, or MeetCap's local model. All follow the same instructions, and you can switch anytime.

- Keep your meetings where you like. Keep them on your computer, or in your own iCloud Drive or OneDrive. Open them on another computer and MeetCap still recognizes the same voices. Put them in an Obsidian vault on iCloud to read minutes on your iPhone.

- Your records are just files. Transcripts and minutes are Markdown files in your own folder. Obsidian opens them, any agent can read them, and they stay put if you stop using MeetCap.

- Recordings stay on your computer. Your audio is transcribed on the computer that recorded it and stays there, even when your minutes sync. Only the transcript text goes to the AI you chose. With a local model, not even the text leaves.

## Built for your AI

Let your agent run MeetCap, or let MeetCap run your agent. Start wherever you already work.

- From your agent. Tell your agent "record this one" and it does. Mid-meeting, ask what you missed. Afterward, get the minutes or find the meeting where the budget came up. Claude Code, Codex, and any agent that can load a skill can do this, right in the chat you already have open.

- From MeetCap. Rather click the menu bar than open a chat? MeetCap runs your agent in the background to write live summaries and minutes. It works with 20+ agents, on the subscription you already have, at no extra cost.

- Your own API key. No agent? Use your own key with the Claude API or any OpenAI-compatible service. Text goes only to the service you set up.

- A local model. MeetCap downloads and sets up a model on your computer. It writes summaries and minutes right there: no key, no account, and no text leaves your computer.

- Find any past meeting by asking. Each meeting is a set of plain files, so any AI that can read your files can find who said what and what was decided.

## Install

Download MeetCap for Mac → Open it and follow the short setup.

Needs a Mac with macOS 14.2 or later, Apple silicon or Intel; Windows and iPhone versions are coming soon.

Prefer the terminal? One line does it:

curl -fsSL https://meetcap.seacen.dev/install.sh | bash

Permissions, models, uninstalling and the rest are covered at meetcap.seacen.dev .

Want something MeetCap doesn't do yet? Check existing suggestions and add a 👍 to the ones you want. To report a problem, suggest something new, or email us, go to the feedback page .

MeetCap is built on open models and software, including X-ASR , sherpa-onnx , Nemotron-3 Diarization , 3D-Speaker , Silero VAD , Gemma and llama.cpp . Thanks to everyone behind them. The full list is in the docs.

# Sevenbox

Sevenbox is causal audit infrastructure for AI agent decisions. A Warrant records why a decision was made: the specific prior claims it depended on, and whether acting on it can be undone. Every call your agent makes becomes one, automatically, the moment you wrap it. When a belief your agent acted on turns out to be wrong, Sevenbox finds exactly what still needs fixing — not by searching logs, by walking the causal chain.

This repo is the open-core layer: the SDK, 14 framework adapters, the local Operations Center UI, and examples. It depends on warrant-core , a separate, compiled engine package — not on PyPI, distributed as a GitHub Release of this repo (see Install and License ).

The local Operations Center UI ( sevenbox ops ) ships with this repo — every run your agent makes, with the causal graph above.

## Install

# Skin: Publishing for AI agents

The web was built around a simple assumption: information is published in a form that people can navigate and read. Websites combine information with its presentation through pages, navigation structures, and language-specific content. AI agents introduce a different kind of consumer, capable of interpreting semantic information and generating responses adapted to individual questions.

Today, agents primarily access information through mechanisms designed to retrieve and interpret existing web content. While these approaches are essential for using the enormous body of information already online, they also inherit the limitations of material originally organized for human consumption.

Skin explores a complementary publication model in which individuals and organizations publish structured semantic information directly for AI agents. Rather than defining how information should be presented, publishers maintain the facts they wish to make available, while consuming agents determine how to interpret and communicate them.

The proposal combines publisher-controlled profiles, atomic semantic facts, a shared schema, and direct retrieval. Its objective is not to replace websites or existing retrieval technologies, but to examine what becomes possible when information can be published for intelligent agents without first being organized into a human-facing interface.

## From websites to information sources

Publishing information online has traditionally meant building a website. Whether introducing a company, describing a product, or explaining a service, publishers organize information into pages, navigation structures, and often multiple language versions.

This organization is largely dictated by how people consume information. Visitors browse, follow links, read explanations, and gradually locate what interests them. Publishers must anticipate those journeys and provide an interface that accommodates them.

Even a relatively simple project can therefore require dozens of pages, navigation categories, and translations. Much of this work concerns not the information itself, but the different ways people might need to access it.

AI agents change that relationship. They can understand questions expressed in natural language, interpret semantic relationships, and construct responses suited to a particular context. Instead of following a publisher's predefined navigation, an agent can identify relevant information and present it directly to its user.

The publisher still needs to make the information available, but no longer necessarily needs to determine how every visitor will navigate or encounter it.

This leads to the question at the center of Skin:

If LLMs can interpret information and generate its presentation, why must publishers first organize that information into websites designed for humans?

Consider a small project that wants to explain what it does, who it serves, how it works, and how to get in touch. A conventional website might distribute those details across an introduction, an about page, several feature pages, and a contact section. The same information might then be translated into multiple languages.

An agent could instead retrieve the underlying information and answer questions about the project directly, without requiring the publisher to anticipate the questions or maintain the pages through which visitors would traditionally find their answers.

Skin proposes treating this underlying information as the publication itself.

A Skin profile is an information source intended for AI agents. Its publisher maintains what is available, while consuming agents decide how to use and communicate it. A profile can exist independently of a website, and the same information can support different agents, interfaces, languages, and use cases.

This is not an attempt to make websites easier to crawl. It is an exploration of how information might be published if a human-facing website were never required in the first place.

## Publishing facts instead of pages

Human-oriented publications typically communicate through prose. A company's website may combine factual statements with explanations, storytelling, promotional language, and visual presentation. This works well for people, but requires AI agents to identify relevant facts within material that was not necessarily written for machine interpretation.

A company might describe itself as a team of passionate innovators delivering cutting-edge solutions. Such language may communicate enthusiasm, but it offers little precise information about the company's actual capabilities.

Skin approaches publication differently, representing information as atomic semantic facts rather than presentation-oriented prose.

The following fragment illustrates how Skin's prototype represents information about the service itself:

{ "profile" : { "name" : " Skin " , "type" : " service " , "facts" : [ { "type" : " capability " , "subject" : " AI agents " , "value" : " retrieve published facts " , "from" : " Skin " , "insteadOf" : " scraped information " }, { "type" : " authoring " , "input" : " natural language conversation " , "output" : " machine-readable index " , "consumer" : " AI agents " } ] } }

The fragment describes two aspects of Skin: how agents can retrieve published information and how that information can be authored. Each fact uses properties appropriate to its meaning, while the shared structure allows an agent to interpret them within the same profile.

The representation describes information without prescribing how an agent should present it. An agent could use these facts to answer questions about Skin, generate a description of its capabilities, or incorporate them into a broader explanation.

Atomicity does not mean reducing every statement to a simplistic three-part relationship. Useful information frequently includes qualifications that are essential to its meaning. A service may be available only in certain countries, a price may depend on specific conditions, or an offer may have a defined validity period. A semantic representation must be able to preserve such context and the relationships between facts, rather than fragmenting them into disconnected statements.

These qualifications belong to the publisher. Skin should allow conditions, scope, and validity periods to be expressed when relevant, without requiring them for every fact or deciding when published information has become obsolete.

The objective is not to eliminate interpretation, which remains necessary even with structured information. It is to reduce the need for agents to extract factual meaning from prose whose primary purpose was human presentation.

### A shared schema

For independent publishers and agents to exchange information, a common structure is necessary. Skin therefore proposes an open schema defining shared fact types, properties, and relationships, while leaving semantic values open to interpretation by language models.

The distinction between structure and semantic values is central to the approach.

A schema can establish that properties such as subject, value, and from serve different roles within a fact without attempting to enumerate every possible subject, value, or source. The structural vocabulary provides consistency, while semantic values remain expressive enough to describe a broad range of activities and relationships.

This is a deliberate trade-off. Comprehensive ontologies can provide precise definitions and strong machine-readable semantics, but they also require extensive vocabularies that must evolve as new domains and concepts emerge.

Skin instead relies partly on the ability of language models to interpret natural-language semantic values within a consistent structure. It does not attempt to standardize every possible concept in advance.

That flexibility introduces uncertainty. Different models may interpret ambiguous values differently, and a shared schema cannot guarantee identical interpretations across consumers. The proposal is therefore not that structure eliminates ambiguity, but that a common structural vocabulary, combined with modern language models, may offer a useful balance between interoperability and expressiveness.

## What changes for publishers

Separating information from presentation changes more than the format in which information is stored. It also changes how publishers control, maintain, and distribute it.

Four properties define the intended publication model.

### Authored

A Skin profile is created and maintained by an authorized publisher. Ownership verification is a prerequisite for creating and publishing a profile, preventing third parties from claiming identities they do not control.

For a domain-associated entity, this means demonstrating control of the corresponding domain. Domain ownership, however, does not imply operating a website: a publisher can control a domain without hosting pages, applications, or other public infrastructure.

Verification establishes authority to publish on behalf of an identity, not the factual accuracy of everything published. A verified company may still publish incomplete, misleading, or incorrect information, just as it can on its own website.

The important distinction is that agents can identify information explicitly published by an entity, rather than relying exclusively on descriptions assembled from external sources.

### Real-time

Web publication and automated retrieval do not necessarily happen at the same time. A publisher may update a page immediately, while crawlers, search indexes, and other intermediate systems continue exposing older versions.

Skin allows publishers to update their information directly at its source, making those changes available without waiting for a crawling or indexing cycle.

This does not guarantee that every agent will immediately consume the latest information. Agents may cache responses or rely on previously retrieved data. Nor does Skin determine whether information is outdated: maintaining published facts remains the publisher's responsibility.

Real-time refers to the availability of changes at the source, not a guarantee that every consumer always holds the latest version.

### No infrastructure

Publishing information for AI agents should not require building and operating a website.

A hosted Skin service can provide the authoring interface, storage, and retrieval mechanisms on behalf of publishers. Individuals and organizations can therefore maintain profiles without deploying servers, developing applications, or implementing their own APIs.

The underlying architecture is intended to remain open, allowing independent implementations and self-hosted services to publish compatible information. The convenience of hosted infrastructure should not become a requirement to use a particular provider.

### Multi-language

Traditional multilingual websites often maintain separate versions of the same information. Each translation must be created, updated, and kept consistent with the others.

Skin proposes publishing semantic facts rather than maintaining language-specific presentations. A consuming agent can interpret those facts and formulate responses in the language appropriate to its user.

This does not guarantee perfect translation or identical wording across languages. Specialized terminology, cultural context, and ambiguous concepts may require additional information, while publishers relinquish some control over the exact language generated by consuming agents.

Nevertheless, the publisher can maintain a shared semantic source rather than repeatedly translating complete pages or predefined answers.

These four properties— Authored, Real-time, No-infra, and Multi-language —follow from a common principle: the publisher maintains information, while consuming agents take responsibility for its presentation.

## The role of the existing web

# solvi

Decision systems you can check. You describe what to compute with plain Python functions and checks; a model — an LLM, your own classifier or a small local one — proposes where judgement is needed; solvi's checks decide. Every answer comes with a confidence, a reason you can check (the rule's inputs, a formula over computed facts, or a quote with character offsets in the source) and a hash-chained trace that can be re-executed later to confirm the answer or pinpoint the step that was altered. When something cannot be computed or checked, solvi abstains or hands the case to a person instead of guessing; a failed hard check always overrides any model's confidence.

solvi 1.0 has two levels. Ready systems you configure: solvi.build (decisions from labelled examples, with a promise on the errors), solvi.Agent (acting in an environment), solvi.Guard (an agent's tool calls) and solvi.Knowledge (what they know, and from whom). Building blocks in solvi.core , which the ready systems are made of, each replaceable by a part of your own. What works but has no measured gain yet is kept apart in solvi.experimental .

## Install

pip install solvi # core: rules, checks, learned answer heads, build / Agent / Guard (numpy, scipy, pydantic) pip install " solvi[model] " # + torch, transformers: ModernBERT field extractors for documents and the decider pip install " solvi[onnx] " # + onnxruntime, tokenizers: the decider (solvi.models.decider) on CPU without torch pip install " solvi[serve] " # + fastapi, uvicorn: `solvi serve app.py:system` — the questions over HTTP (also --mcp) pip install " solvi[mcp] " # + the official MCP SDK for solvi serve --mcp (without it, a built-in stdio server) pip install " solvi[duckdb] " # + duckdb: stored decisions in a DuckDB file (solvi.core.store.DuckDBStorage); [postgres] for PostgreSQL pip install " solvi[lora] " # + torch, transformers, peft: solvi.experimental.lora.adapt_lora, a LoRA adapter per question (experimental)

Requires Python 3.11+ (tested on 3.11–3.14). Coming from 0.9: see below .

## Start

### Decisions: solvi.build

Give the question, labelled examples and the promise — and a slow path if you have one. solvi.build fits System 1, calibrates its guarantee and who answers what it hands over on examples it did not see, stores every decision, and says what it chose:

import solvi from solvi . models import llm s = solvi . build ( question , examples , catalog = cat , max_risk = 0.02 , # examples: [(state, correct answer)] slow = llm ( URL , "openai/gpt-oss-120b" ), price = ( 0.037 , 0.17 ), storage = "decisions.jsonl" ) res = s . ask ( state ) # res.answer, res.by ("s1", "s2" or "human"), res.reasons, res.cost print ( s . explain ()) # System 1, its signal and promise, who answers each slice, what is not covered

On four tasks of the stand (Banking77, Abt-Buy, CUAD, RAGTruth) the defaults matched or beat the hand-written setups with every promise kept on eval, in a quarter to half of the code — closer to the promised level than the hand-written ones, and the slow path was rarely given anything ( guide , examples/24_one_entry_point.py ).

### Environments: solvi.Agent and solvi.Knowledge

km = solvi . Knowledge ( "knowledge.jsonl" , vocabulary = { "here" : lambda s , a : s [ "here" ], "wood" : lambda s , a : s [ "wood" ]}) km . goal ( "table" , done = lambda s : s [ "table" ]) # an agenda goal: done is code agent = solvi . Agent ( env , knowledge = km ) # env: reset(seed), actions(state), step(action) → Outcome agent . run ( seed = 7 , steps = 150 ) # explore; the same world again needs fewer slow decisions agent . replay () # every decision re-checked from what it was given

solvi.Knowledge keeps what a system learned and from whom: facts with their sources (never the system's own answers), goals and gates, an action model learned from outcomes; a retraction takes back everything derived from the item. solvi.Agent acts on it: System 1 where the knowledge predicts the action works, a search where it does not, gates and predicted refusals as hard checks — protection by default, justified risk ( RiskBudget ) as an option. In the toy crafting world of examples/25_environment_agent.py the first run takes 61 steps, all decided by System 2, and the same world met again 12 steps, 11 of them by System 1. Growth was shown in environments met again, not on decision streams or a support agent with tools; justified risk lowers the cost of protection without promising parity ( docs/agent.md ). solvi.build(..., knowledge=km) and solvi.Guard(..., knowledge=km) read the same knowledge.

### Tool calls: solvi.Guard

The agent proposes {"name": tool, "arguments": {...}} ; solvi.Guard checks it — the tool is in the catalog, the arguments validate against its types, the values that must come from the conversation are quoted there (and not only from a tool output that says "ignore previous instructions"), your policies (limits, roles, allow-lists) are ordinary hard checks, and an optional decider asks "did the user ask for this?" under act_guard and perturb — then allows it (solvi runs the function), denies it with the reasons, or escalates it to a person. Every decision is a stored, replayable trace; any framework's tool calls go through guard.check / guard.call ( guide , examples/19_agent_guard.py ). On τ-bench retail no call it let through was refused by the environment, at a cost in solved tasks (the τ-bench row of the task table ).

### Models: solvi.models

Types declare questions; a model proposes; checks decide. The fields of a pydantic model are the questions, their types the kinds (one option, several, an ordered score, yes/no); a decider answers them about a text or a JSON / pydantic state with probabilities, a calibrated confidence and act / escalate, and hard checks, constraints and rules still decide. The decider is whichever model you have:

- An LLM — solvi.models.llm(base_url, model, api_key=...) : any OpenAI-compatible chat-completions server (OpenAI, OpenRouter, vLLM, llama.cpp, Ollama). Nothing to install beyond the core; its JSON replies are validated, and an invalid one escalates, never a guess.

- A decision service — solvi.models.systemone(url, model) : anything that speaks the System One API.

- A local checkpoint, for offline or cheap cases — solvi.models.decider("solvi-base") ( solvi[onnx] , no GPU; solvi models pull solvi-ai/solvi-base downloads it). solvi-base is a 150M ModernBERT-base cross-encoder distilled from solvi-large: about 50 ms per question on a CPU (ONNX fp16, 4 threads). Its card is honest about where it stands: 54.5% zero-shot on typed questions over JSON states (the same as solvi-large), 56.3% on Fast Decisions dev — not better than earlier small models there — and 0.602 on the jabr classifier benchmark, where Jev reaches 0.966. A preview: fit it on 30–60 labelled examples of your task and calibrate its escalation on your own stream before relying on it.

import os from typing import Literal from pydantic import BaseModel , Field from solvi import Catalog , Scale , System from solvi . models import llm class Triage ( BaseModel ): team : Literal [ "billing" , "technical" , "shipping" ] = Field ( description = "Which team should handle this ticket?" ) urgency : Scale [ Literal [ "low" , "medium" , "high" , "critical" ]] = Field ( description = "How urgent is it?" ) angry : bool = Field ( description = "Is the customer angry?" ) topics : list [ Literal [ "refund" , "delay" , "bug" ]] = Field ( description = "What does the ticket mention?" ) model = llm ( "https://api.openai.com/v1" , "gpt-4o-mini" , api_key = os . environ [ "OPENAI_API_KEY" ]) # offline: model = solvi.models.decider("solvi-base") — the same questions, the same checks cat = Catalog () questions = model . questions ( cat , Triage , text_fact = "ticket" , min_confidence = 0.6 ) @ cat . check ( hard = True , then = { "urgency" : "critical" }) # a legal threat is critical, whatever the model says def no_legal_threat ( ticket ) -> bool : return "lawyer" not in str ( ticket ). lower () questions [ 1 ]. requires . append ( "no_legal_threat" ) res = System ( cat , questions ). ask ({ "ticket" : { "subject" : "Charged twice" , "body" : "Refund my double payment!" , "customer" : { "tier" : "pro" }}}) print ({ q : ( r . answer , r . status ) for q , r in res . results . items ()}) print ( res . audit ( "team" )) # the probabilities, the model's fingerprint, what escalated and why

A state is read as key paths ( customer.tier: pro ); an unsure or escalated answer abstains with the reason ( system.stats["model_escalated"] , ["low_confidence"] ). examples/15_typed_decisions.py runs the whole story with a stand-in model, without network. Whatever the model, read what it was measured on before relying on it, and calibrate it on your own labelled stream ( part.act_guard , under Building blocks): checks, constraints and escalation are what make the answers safe to act on, not the model alone. The checkpoint contract of a local decider is in docs/decide_format.md ; a local checkpoint answers one question per forward pass with the published checkpoints, several with DecideModel.load(..., multi_question=True) .

Every answer is a value and a confidence, and the types also declare answer primitives: Maybe[T] ("not stated" — solvi.Unknown — is a real answer, unlike an abstention), Span[float] (an exact piece of the text, parsed), Rank[...] (the top k, in order), Estimate[0, 7, 14] (a number with an interval), and evidence quotes on any answer ( Claim(value, evidence=[...]) , Question(require_evidence=True) ) — each checked in the text, from rules or a model ( guide , examples/16_primitives.py ).

### The open decision compiler

Compile your intent once with an LLM. Then decide on every record forever — classification, scoring, routing — as type-safe JSON with probabilities and confidence, on your own hardware, at zero marginal cost .

Website · Docs · Benchmarks · PyPI

Agents at compile time. Never at runtime.

import strot result = strot . run ( tickets , query = "Triage incoming support tickets into the correct workflow." , action_registry = { "billing_dispute" : "Refunds, invoice corrections, double charges" , "technical_defect" : "Crashes, bugs, broken behavior" , }, llm = "anthropic/claude-opus-4-8" , # used once, on first compile only ) for o in result . outcomes : print ( o [ "action" ], round ( o [ "confidence" ], 2 )) # billing_dispute 0.97 # technical_defect 0.94

The LLM runs once , at compile time. Production is a frozen, self-contained Python artifact: a small local decision model arbitrates every record, nothing is generated, every output is bounded, and low-confidence records abstain instead of guessing.

STROT = Agentic Schema Intent + Compiler & State + Code + Execution + NLU ⟹ JSON Decisions (classification · scoring · routing · typed answers)

## How it works

COMPILE (once per intent + schema) intent + sample ─▶ synthesize ─▶ golden gate ─▶ teacher labels ─▶ calibrate (labels, (your known (annotate (fit the projection, answers must a sample, confidence handlers) pass) once) threshold) │ ▼ frozen artifact (.py) RUNTIME (every record, forever) record ─▶ projection ─▶ decision model ─▶ confidence gate ─▶ typed JSON (compiled) (144M, CPU, (decide or decision ~60 ms) abstain)

run() — route each record to an action and execute the compiled handler.

decide() — answer typed questions (choice / score / boolean) per record:

Real model (SupersonicLabs/Julia-1, 144M, CPU), real datasets, clean Docker containers:

Reproduce everything: benchmarks/ — with the losses published too.

- Compile once, decide forever — content-addressed artifact cache; schema drift triggers exactly one recompile.

- Golden-record promotion — artifacts must pass your known answers before they serve.

- Fitted guarantees — temperature scaling + split conformal prediction, baked in: dispatched decisions are wrong ≤ α of all records (marginal); the rest abstain.

- Measured, not guessed — the compiler scores labelings, and can train a distilled head, keeping only what beats the baseline on held-out data.

# sturnus

Automatic latency-based routing across LLM providers. A single static binary, zero infrastructure.

LLM providers have variable latency and availability that can break production features. sturnus is a lightweight sidecar that sits beside your app, exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, and automatically shifts traffic to whichever provider is fastest and available right now.

## Quick start

sturnus needs a config.toml — copy config.example.toml and add your providers.

Docker — best for production deployments and Kubernetes sidecars:

docker run -v ./config.toml:/config.toml \ -p 4000:4000 \ ghcr.io/sturnus-dev/sturnus:latest

cargo install — best for local testing if you have a Rust toolchain:

cargo install sturnus sturnus --config config.toml

Prebuilt static binaries for Linux and macOS (x86_64 and aarch64) are attached to every release .

Then point any OpenAI-compatible SDK at sturnus — the only change is the base URL:

- client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.openai.com/v1", api_key="sk-...") + client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1", api_key="unused")

from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI ( base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1" , api_key = "unused" ) response = client . chat . completions . create ( model = "fast" , # resolved by sturnus to the fastest available candidate messages = [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "Hello" }], )

## Features

- Latency- and error-aware routing — the fastest healthy provider gets the bulk of traffic, while slower or erroring ones keep a small, shrinking share. That share doubles as a probe, so a recovered provider wins its traffic back automatically, with no thresholds to trip.

- Session affinity — a stateless x-session-affinity header pins follow-up requests to the same provider across pods.

- Transparent passthrough — only the model field is rewritten: the request body is otherwise forwarded byte-for-byte, preserving key order, number precision, and formatting. Responses, including SSE text/event-stream chunks, are relayed untouched as they arrive.

- Memory-bounded — request buffers are capped per request and in aggregate; bursts beyond the memory budget shed load with 429 + Retry-After instead of OOMing the pod.

- Vertex AI support — GKE Workload Identity auth via the metadata server, with automatic token refresh.

- Zero infrastructure — a single static binary; no Redis, database, or control plane.

## Why sturnus

Most LLM gateways are either a hosted SaaS you route all your traffic (and keys) through, or a large application with a significant surface area. sturnus is the opposite — a single static binary with a small auditable surface area, MIT-licensed and running entirely inside your infrastructure. It speaks the OpenAI API, so any OpenAI-compatible SDK works by changing one base URL. The core capability of sturnus is automatic latency-based routing across providers — something that most gateways put behind an enterprise tier. Each sidecar routes independently from what it observes locally, so there is no shared state to run.

If you need a full LLMOps platform (spend tracking, prompt management, a UI, dozens of integrations), sturnus is not that.

sturnus has a bounded scope by design and has some deliberate omissions:

- No request-level failover or retries. sturnus is a transparent proxy: it surfaces upstream errors to the client verbatim rather than silently retrying within a black box. Error responses still feed the routing signal, so a flaky provider is quickly deprioritized for subsequent traffic — but the individual failed request is returned as-is. Client SDKs (OpenAI, Anthropic, LangChain, etc.) already ship mature, configurable retry and backoff; configure it there and let sturnus steer those retries toward the healthiest provider.

- Latency-based, not cost or quality-based. Routing optimizes time-to-first-chunk within an alias , and every model routed under that alias should be largely interchangeable. sturnus never trades quality or cost for speed — it just picks the fastest among options you've already deemed equivalent.

## Contents

- Configuration

- Endpoints

- Observability

- Session affinity

- How routing works

- Docker

- Building

Prometheus metrics on /metrics , all labelled by alias , provider , model :

Connection failures are zero-initialised at startup so a missing series is never mistaken for "no errors".

### Logging

Structured logging via tracing : coloured text on a terminal (respecting NO_COLOR ), newline-delimited JSON when piped or redirected. Set the format with --log-format <auto|pretty|json> (or STURNUS_LOG_FORMAT ) and the level with RUST_LOG (default sturnus=info ).

Each request gets a span with a request_id ; a client-supplied W3C traceparent propagates as trace_id and parent_span_id for cross-service correlation.

Every response includes an x-session-affinity header (e.g. openai/gpt-4o-mini ). Pass it back on subsequent requests to pin to the same provider — useful for multi-turn conversations where context is provider-specific:

response = client . chat . completions . create ( model = "fast" , messages = [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "Hello" }], ) affinity = response . headers [ "x-session-affinity" ] # e.g. "openai/gpt-4o-mini" response = client . chat . completions . create ( model = "fast" , messages = [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "Follow-up" }], extra_headers = { "x-session-affinity" : affinity }, )

Fully stateless — works across pods with no shared state. The pin is honored until the pinned candidate's error-rate EWMA breaches error_threshold (at the default smoothing, roughly two consecutive errors), at which point the header is ignored and a new provider is selected — check the updated x-session-affinity in the response. Unknown or malformed headers fall back to normal routing.

- Client sends POST /v1/chat/completions with "model": "fast" .

- Sidecar looks up the fast alias and computes each candidate's effective latency : its latency EWMA divided by its success-rate EWMA. A candidate erroring with probability p needs ~ 1/(1-p) attempts per success, so errors inflate effective latency the same way slowness does.

- Each candidate is weighted by (best_effective / its_effective)^k , so the best gets the bulk of traffic and worse ones a shrinking-but-nonzero share. A deterministic low-discrepancy sequence (golden-ratio Weyl sequence) turns those weights into picks.

- Because worse candidates always keep a small share, their EWMAs stay fresh — a provider that recovers (faster responses or errors stopping) wins traffic back automatically; a cold candidate (no latency data yet) probes at a quarter of the best candidate's rate, scaled by its success rate, until its first samples land.

- The model field is rewritten to the real model name, auth headers are set, and the request is forwarded.

- TTFC is measured at first chunk arrival and fed back into the EWMA; the response status (any non-2xx counts as an error, including upstream 4xx) feeds the success-rate EWMA.

The best provider is exploited heavily while worse ones keep enough traffic to stay measured. A candidate's probe share shrinks with how bad it looks but is floored at 1%, so re-detecting a recovered provider costs at most ~100 requests — and during an outage at most ~1% of an alias's traffic is spent on the failing candidate.

- Kubernetes native sidecar (recommended): the app container shares the pod's network namespace and reaches sturnus on 127.0.0.1:4000 , so keep listen = "127.0.0.1:4000" — bound to loopback, the credential-bearing proxy is unreachable from other pods entirely. To scrape metrics, set metrics_listen = "0.0.0.0:4040" : it serves only /metrics , /health , /healthz and /status (never the proxy) on the routable pod IP, and stays up until the proxy has finished draining so the final scrape window isn't lost. Containers in a pod share ports, so pick a metrics port the app doesn't use.

- Standalone Docker with the client in a separate container: it reaches sturnus over the container's IP, which a 127.0.0.1 bind refuses, so listen must be 0.0.0.0:4000 .

On Kubernetes, run sturnus as a native sidecar — an init container with restartPolicy: Always (stable since v1.29). It then starts before the app container and is terminated after it, so the proxy is ready for the app's first request and stays up while the app drains.

Memory needs no tuning: the aggregate request-buffer budget defaults to half the container's memory limit (read from cgroups at startup, logged with its source), so a small sidecar sheds excess load with 429 s rather than getting OOM-killed. # AI Service Indicators

A community-maintained list of DNS hostnames for generative-AI applications and APIs, for measuring observed AI-service access from DNS, proxy or firewall logs.

Each row maps a hostname pattern to a service, vendor, category and role, so you can tell chat use from API calls, agents, sign-in, CDN, telemetry and plain website visits. Where a vendor publishes the hostname, the row links to that page.

> A DNS lookup shows a device contacted a service, not that anyone submitted a prompt. Report results as observed access, count distinct devices rather than queries, and remember that devices are not people.

## The data

data/ai_services.csv

### Roles

### Confidence

confidence describes the role. A source on a catch-all or hostname row shows that the domain belongs to the vendor, not what each subdomain does. Corrections backed by vendor documentation are especially welcome.

Using role , you can tell, for example, ChatGPT chat ( chatgpt.com , ws.chatgpt.com ) apart from OpenAI API calls ( api.openai.com ), Codex agents ( codex-cloud-backend.chatgpt.com ), and someone reading openai.com or help.openai.com .

No field contains a comma or quote, so any CSV reader, awk -F, , or a SIEM lookup can load the file as-is.

### Matching rules

- Lowercase the queried hostname and strip any trailing dot.

- Try rows in file order ; the first matching row wins. Specific names come before their wildcard catch-alls ( api.openai.com before *.openai.com ).

- A pattern matches the whole hostname: *.chatgpt.com matches ab.chatgpt.com but not fakechatgpt.com or chatgpt.com.example.net . Apex domains are listed separately.

- A hostname matching no row is not in scope.

These are the semantics of a Splunk WILDCARD lookup with max_matches=1 .

## How to interpret results

- Report by role , not by domain. Telemetry and experiment names (for example ab.chatgpt.com ) fire on page load and are often queried by more devices than the app itself. There is no blanket "all openai.com = ChatGPT" rule.

- An API hostname identifies the service contacted, not the application, person, model or billing account behind it. api.anthropic.com , for example, is used by Claude Code as well as by custom applications.

- A usage role shows that a service was in use on a device, not what the person did with it. DNS cannot show whether someone generated an image, ran an agent or only opened the app.

- Some vendor names are reached from other companies' websites. bzr.openai.com , for example, is OpenAI's ad-measurement pixel, embedded in advertisers' sites, and is queried by devices that never use ChatGPT.

- Keep non-usage roles out of usage counts. auth , cdn , telemetry and web names can corroborate activity, but browsers prefetch them, and they are reached by people who never use the product.

- Count distinct devices per service per day or week, not queries. Caching, retries, background refresh and prefetching distort query counts.

- Classify the name the client asked for , not CDN alias (CNAME) targets in the response.

### Coverage gaps

DNS-based measurement misses:

- off-network devices;

- clients using encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT) to outside resolvers;

- locally run models;

- AI features embedded in other SaaS products, which share the host application's hostnames;

- calls made from a vendor's backend.

Some services (OpenRouter, Azure AI Foundry, Bedrock, Vertex AI) front many models, and DNS cannot tell which model was used.

## Using it

Implement the matching rules above. For each pattern, a regex of ^ + the pattern with * replaced by .* (everything else escaped) + $ is enough. In Splunk, load the CSV as a lookup with match_type = WILDCARD(host_pattern) and max_matches = 1 .

On high-volume DNS indexes, filter on indexed terms before classifying: python3 scripts/splunk_terms.py prints a keyword filter that covers every pattern.

## Contributing

New services, endpoints and corrections are welcome. See CONTRIBUTING.md . Every change must pass python3 scripts/validate.py , which also runs automatically on pull requests.

# TenseMem

Memory that knows its tenses. Embedded, deterministic memory that AI agents can safely act on.

One SQLite file. No server required. The model proposes typed facts; the engine decides what is current.

pip install tensemem

from tensemem import FakeExtractor , Memory mem = Memory ( llm = FakeExtractor ()) mem . register_predicate ( "lives_in" ) added = mem . add ( "u1" , "I live in Delhi" ) ctx = mem . context ( user_id = "u1" , min_seq = added . seq , wait = 1.5 ) print ( ctx . text ) # fenced block the model can read print ( ctx . freshness . is_current ) # True once extract finished

FakeExtractor is rule-based and needs no API key. Same API with tensemem[openai] , tensemem[anthropic] , tensemem[ollama] , tensemem[litellm] , or Gemini ( GEMINI_API_KEY in the process environment).

## Why this exists

Similarity search returns both “I live in Delhi” and “I moved to Bangalore” and leaves the model to guess. TenseMem keeps one current value per slot, says whether the read is fresh, and refuses to learn from its own output.

- One current truth per ONE slot. A new city supersedes the old one. History still answers “where did I live before?”

- Every read reports freshness. as_of_seq , pending , is_current . Wait for a message, or see that it is not applied yet.

- No self-echo. Recalled context() is fenced. Extract needs a verbatim quote from the user.

- Corrections stick. correct() restores the displaced value and survives rebuild() with a newer model.

- The engine decides. The LLM emits typed ops. Deterministic rules apply them.

- No infrastructure. Default store is one SQLite file inside your process.

## Delhi, then Bangalore

mem . add ( "u1" , "I live in Delhi" ) mem . set ( user_id = "u1" , predicate = "lives_in" , value = "Bangalore" ) print ( mem . state ( "u1" ). values ) # {"lives_in": "Bangalore"} history = mem . history ( "u1" , predicate = "lives_in" ) # ACTIVE Bangalore, SUPERSEDED Delhi bangalore = next ( f for f in history . facts if f . object == "Bangalore" ) mem . correct ( bangalore . id ) # that move was never true print ( mem . state ( "u1" ). values ) # {"lives_in": "Delhi"}

# Tessary

Stop your agents from failing silently in production.

Docs · Self-host · Report an issue · Discussions

Tessary is an open-source reliability platform for AI agents in production. It monitors every trace, detects issues using cheap classifiers, groups related findings into cases, and investigates their root cause using trace and repository evidence.

## Get running

To try it without installing anything, sign up for Tessary Cloud at https://app.tessary.ai . It's free, needs no credit card, and its limits are on the pricing page .

To self-host, paste this into your coding agent:

Self-host Tessary for me by following https://github.com/tessaryai/tessary/blob/main/setup.md

setup.md is written as instructions to an agent: install what's missing, bring every service up, verify the frontend, and hand back the URL.

Prefer to run it yourself? The same install is one command, with nothing cloned and no .env to edit:

docker compose -f oci://docker.io/tessaryai/tessary:compose up -d -y

Either way, open http://localhost when docker compose -p tessary ps reports every service healthy. It needs Docker Engine 26 or newer and Docker Compose v2.34 or newer on the machine. Set up Tessary takes it from there.

Once it's running, instrument your agent so Tessary has traces to watch: see the instrumentation overview .

### 1. Point your agent's traces at it

Send OTLP traces to the endpoint shown during setup and add tessary.call_site.id to spans that invoke a model. Use instrument.md to have a coding agent identify and instrument these call sites.

### 2. Connect the repo (optional)

Connect a GitHub repository under Settings > Git integration and both triage and RCA cite the code that produced the failing traces.

## How it works

- Watch every trace. OTLP over HTTP and gRPC, and SDK push, normalize to the OpenTelemetry gen_ai.* conventions at the edge. PII (personally identifiable information) redaction runs before storage.

- Filter cheaply. Classifiers sweep every trace continuously and open a finding when one fires. The per-trace check stays cheap enough to afford at production volume, which is what makes reading all of it possible instead of sampling. Two classifiers are exceptions, and both are off until you turn them on: frustration scores eligible user messages with a hosted model on your own OpenRouter or TypeSafe key, and groundedness checks answers against their retrieved documents with a public model you run on a Mac with Apple silicon or a GPU instance on AWS, not an LLM call.

- Group into cases. Related findings collapse into one case, surfaced on Triage . An LLM triage step rules whether a finding is a real deviation rather than a legitimate change, and only a finding it rules real becomes a case. Two kinds of finding are ruled when they are filed instead, because their numbers are the claim: a high-confidence secret leak, and a rise in frustrated conversations.

- Explain the case. RCA runs an agentic session over the failing traces and, when a repo is connected, the code itself. It returns a one-sentence summary, the causes it found with the traces behind each, and the checks it ruled out.

- Route it to a human. An alert carries the case to whoever owns it. Tessary explains and hands off. It doesn't open the fix.

## Telemetry

A self-hosted instance sends one anonymous heartbeat to home.tessary.ai at backend start and every 6 hours after. It carries a schema version, an install id, a ping sequence number, a timestamp, the edition, the app version, the host OS family and CPU architecture, install-wide totals of projects, ingested spans, findings, cases, and classifier detections, and the hash of the model price book it holds. On the same schedule it checks home.tessary.ai for a newer price book and downloads it only when the hash has changed. It never carries trace or prompt content, an email address, an org or project name, a hostname, or a retained IP address.

TESSARY_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false
